title: Managing a Rules-Based Leader
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article profiles the "rules-based leader," who finds security in strict adherence to policy, procedure, and hierarchy, and contrasts this style sharply with value-driven leadership, which uses principles flexibly to navigate nuance. It explains why this style frustrates colleagues who prefer creative or risk-tolerant approaches, since rules-based leaders resist departures from convention and can stifle candid discussion. While acknowledging genuine advantages, fairness, clarity, predictability, the piece pivots to practical advice for working with such a leader: use their own respect for authority and expertise against the friction, by bringing in outside experts, building advocacy with more senior figures first, or invoking a superseding rule. It closes with a wry callback that the "number one rule" for managing a rules-based leader is not to forget the strategy itself.
points: Rules-based leadership prioritizes strict adherence to policy and hierarchy, which produces predictability but also rigidity and resistance to nuance.
The key distinction from value-driven leadership is that values flex to navigate complexity, while rules apply uniformly regardless of context.
Rules-based leaders defer to expertise and authority, so bringing outside subject-matter voices is an effective way to influence their thinking.
Building advocacy with more senior figures before proposing new ideas is another practical lever for working around a rules-based leader's resistance.
quotes: Rules-based leaders find security in strictly following rules and comfort by deferring to authority.
A value-driven leader depends upon bedrock principles and values to guide their actions and decisions.
This brand of leadership style can be off-putting for those who want to work through issues and grapple with the complexity of situations without such a black-and-white lens.
Because they hold status, authority, and hierarchy in such high regard, rules-based leaders also defer to expertise.
Think also about building advocacy with those more senior to them before introducing ideas or proposing solutions.
